17.4 The stock market

The same comparison of returns tells us what a share of stock is worth. Here we compare the model’s price-earnings ratio with more than a century of U.S. stock-market data.

Fig. 3: The price-earnings ratio in the stock market

Goal. Read the price-earnings ratio of the U.S. stock market with the arbitrage equation for stocks.

Robert Shiller’s price-earnings (P/E) ratio divides the S&P 500 stock price index by the average real earnings of its companies over the previous ten years. Equation (10) says what the ratio should be: the payout ratio divided by \(R-g\). The teal line in the figure is this model ratio. With the textbook’s numbers from the stock example, \(R = 5\) percent and \(g = 2\) percent, and a payout ratio of one half, the model ratio is \(0.5/0.03 \approx 16.7\), close to the long-run average.

This figure stays U.S.-only: Shiller’s monthly data are the only free, long series of a ten-year P/E ratio. Ratios for other stock markets are sold by commercial data providers and cannot be shared here.

# Load Shiller's monthly P/E ratio; `.tail(3)` shows the last three rows
cape = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig17-3.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
cape.tail(3)
date cape cape_average
1747 2026-08-01 40.9874 17.8044
1748 2026-09-01 40.5809 17.8044
1749 2026-10-01 40.7106 17.8044

Each row is a month. cape is the P/E ratio and cape_average its average over all months since 1881. parse_dates=["date"] turns the text in the date column into real dates.

First the numbers of the figure. pe_summary takes the latest month and the long-run average from the data, and computes the model ratio of equation (10).

def pe_summary(R, g, payout):
    """The latest P/E ratio, its average, and the model ratio (Fig. 3).

    Equation (10):  P/E = payout / (R - g), which has no finite value when g >= R

    Arguments
        R      : real interest rate, R
        g      : growth rate of the dividend, g
        payout : the payout ratio, dividend / earnings
    Returns
        last    : the last row of `cape`, the latest month
        average : the average P/E ratio over all months since 1881
        model   : the model P/E ratio of equation (10), or None when g >= R
    """
    # `cape.iloc[-1]` is the last row of the table (`iloc` picks rows by position)
    last, average = cape.iloc[-1], cape.cape.mean()
    # `if R > g:` runs the indented line only when the condition holds, and `else:`
    # handles the other case. Equation (9) has no finite price when g >= R, so this
    # also keeps us from dividing by zero
    if R > g:
        model = pe_ratio(payout, R, g)
    else:
        model = None
    return last, average, model
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, the model line and its label
def add_pe_model(fig, R, g, payout, model, last):
    """Draw the teal model line of Fig. 3 and its label, when R > g.

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        R      : real interest rate, R
        g      : growth rate of the dividend, g
        payout : the payout ratio, dividend / earnings
        model  : the model P/E ratio (None when g >= R)
        last   : the last row of `cape`, the latest month
    Returns
        the text about the model for the title
    """
    model_text = "model: no finite price, because g ≥ R"
    if R > g:
        # the flat teal line at the model ratio, across all the years
        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=[cape.date.iloc[0], last.date],
                y=[model, model],
                mode="lines",
                name="Model, equation (10)",
                line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3),
            )
        )
        model_text = f"model: {payout:.2f} / ({R:.1%} − {g:.2%}) = {model:.1f}"
        # a one-line if: `a if condition else b` gives a when the condition holds
        # and b otherwise. A model line above the chart is not visible: point up
        label = "Model" if model < 48 else "Model ↑"
        # its label at the right end; `min(model, 48)` keeps it inside the chart
        fig.add_annotation(
            x=last.date,
            y=min(model, 48),
            text=label,
            showarrow=False,
            xanchor="left",
            xshift=6,
            font=dict(color=TEAL, size=14),
        )
    return model_text
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, the price-earnings ratio in the stock market
def pe_chart(R=0.05, g=0.02, payout=0.5):
    """The P/E ratio, its average, and the model ratio payout / (R - g).

    Draws Fig. 3 (inspired by Fig. 17.3 in Jones), with the model line of
    equation (10).

    Arguments
        R      : real interest rate, R
        g      : growth rate of the dividend, g
        payout : the payout ratio, dividend / earnings
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (pe_summary)
    last, average, model = pe_summary(R, g, payout)

    # Step 2: `px.area` draws the P/E ratio as a line and fills the area below it
    fig = px.area(
        cape,
        x="date",
        y="cape",
        color_discrete_sequence=["#5aa0d8"],
        labels={"date": "Year", "cape": "P/E ratio"},
    )
    # the dashed black line: the average since 1881, and its label
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[cape.date.iloc[0], last.date],
            y=[average, average],
            mode="lines",
            name="Average",
            line=dict(color="black", width=1.5, dash="dash"),
        )
    )
    fig.add_annotation(
        x="1981-01-01",
        y=average + 7,
        text=f"Mean 1881–{last.date.year}: {average:.1f}",
        showarrow=False,
        font=dict(size=14),
    )

    # Step 3: the model line (add_pe_model), then the title and fixed axes
    model_text = add_pe_model(fig, R, g, payout, model, last)
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"P/E ratio {last.cape:.1f} in {last.date:%b %Y}  |  {model_text}",
        # up to 2041: room for the label on the right
        xaxis=dict(range=["1881-01-01", "2041-01-01"]),
        yaxis=dict(range=[0, 50], tickvals=[0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50]),
        showlegend=False,
    )
    return fig

The model line is our own, from equation (10). Prepared file: data/ch17/fig17-3.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 17.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The ratio is very volatile. It peaked in September 1929, before the crash, and reached its record, 44.2, in December 1999 at the top of the dot-com boom (the textbook dates this peak “in 2001”; by 2001 the ratio had already fallen to between 28 and 37). It was below 7 in 1920 and in 1982.
  • In 2026 the ratio climbed back to about 40, close to the 1999 record.
  • With the slider, the model line rises slowly at first and then very fast: a P/E ratio of 40 needs \(R-g = 1.25\) percent, against 3 percent for 16.7. Small changes in expected growth or in the interest rate can justify big changes in stock prices. That is why it is hard to tell a bubble from a change in the fundamentals.

Key numbers: averages, peaks and the growth rate the market expects

The textbook prints an average of 17.4. That is the average up to March 2023, the last month in the textbook’s figure. With the data up to today the average is a little higher.

# Step 1: the average P/E ratio up to the textbook's last month, and up to today
book_sample = cape[cape.date <= "2023-03-01"]
print(
    f"Average P/E ratio, 1881 to March 2023: {book_sample.cape.mean():.1f}"
    "   (textbook: 17.4)"
)
print(f"Average P/E ratio, 1881 to {cape.date.iloc[-1]:%B %Y}: {cape.cape.mean():.1f}")
# Step 2: the peak month of 1929 and of 1999 (`idxmax` gives the row label of the
# largest value, and `.loc` picks that row)
for year in [1929, 1999]:
    top = cape.loc[cape[cape.date.dt.year == year].cape.idxmax()]
    print(f"Peak of {year}: {top.cape:.1f} in {top.date:%B %Y}")
Average P/E ratio, 1881 to March 2023: 17.4   (textbook: 17.4)
Average P/E ratio, 1881 to October 2026: 17.8
Peak of 1929: 32.6 in September 1929
Peak of 1999: 44.2 in December 1999

Turn equation (10) around: for a given payout ratio, the P/E ratio tells us the value of \(R-g\) that the market’s price implies, \(R - g = \text{payout}/(P/E)\).

# The R - g implied by a P/E ratio: R - g = payout / (P/E), equation (10) turned around
last = cape.iloc[-1]
# for the long-run average and for the latest month
for name, ratio in [
    ("the long-run average", cape.cape.mean()),
    (f"{last.date:%B %Y}", last.cape),
]:
    print(
        f"P/E ratio of {ratio:.1f} ({name}): R - g = {0.5 / ratio:.2%} "
        "with a payout ratio of 0.5"
    )
P/E ratio of 17.8 (the long-run average): R - g = 2.81% with a payout ratio of 0.5
P/E ratio of 40.7 (October 2026): R - g = 1.23% with a payout ratio of 0.5

Today’s prices are consistent with the simple model only if investors expect dividends to grow almost as fast as the interest rate. Either they do, or prices are above their fundamental value.

17.5 Investment in the data

Finally, we split U.S. private investment into its parts and see which ones move most in booms and recessions, in the United States and in other countries.

Fig. 4: Components of private investment (as a share of GDP)

Goal. See which parts of investment move most in recessions.

In the national accounts, private investment has three parts:

  • nonresidential fixed investment: equipment and structures bought by businesses, and intellectual property products such as research and software;
  • residential fixed investment: new housing;
  • inventory investment: the change in the stock of goods that firms have produced but not yet sold.
# Load the three tables of Fig. 4: annual shares, recession dates, quarterly shares
invest = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig17-4.csv")
recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])
quarterly = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "investment_quarterly.csv", parse_dates=["date"])

Each row of invest is a year, and each column a share of GDP in percent; total is the sum of the three parts. recessions lists the U.S. recessions dated by the NBER, and quarterly has the total and residential shares for every quarter.

To draw all the parts with one px.line call, Plotly Express wants a long table: one row per year and component. We first give the columns readable names, which then appear in the legend.

# Step 1: readable names for the columns; `.rename(columns=...)` renames columns
# with a dictionary
NAMES = {
    "total": "Total",
    "nonres_fixed": "Nonresidential fixed",
    "residential": "Residential",
    "inventories": "Inventory",
}
invest = invest.rename(columns=NAMES)

# Step 2: the long table. `.melt(id_vars="year")` turns a wide table into a long one:
# the column names go into a new column (`component`), the values into another
# (`share`)
annual_long = invest.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="component", value_name="share")
# `pd.to_datetime(...)` turns the year into a date (1 January), so that the years
# line up with the recession dates
annual_long["date"] = pd.to_datetime(annual_long.year.astype(str))

# Step 3: the same for the quarterly data since 1975
recent = quarterly[quarterly.date >= "1975-01-01"].rename(columns=NAMES)
quarterly_long = recent.melt(id_vars="date", var_name="component", value_name="share")
# the lowest quarter of 2009 (`idxmin` gives the row label of the smallest value)
low = recent.loc[recent[recent.date.dt.year == 2009].Total.idxmin()]

The chart needs no new economics, so its code is all drawing code. shade_recessions shades the recessions, with one shaded rectangle (add_vrect) from the peak to the trough of each recession, and components_chart draws one line per component from the annual or the quarterly table; its quarterly title reports low.

Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, the colors and the recession bands
# one color per component, the same for every country
COLORS = {
    "Total": BLUE,
    "Nonresidential fixed": GREEN,
    "Residential": TEAL,
    "Inventory": "#5aa0d8",
}


def shade_recessions(fig, start):
    """Shade every NBER recession that ends after the date start.

    Draws the recession bands of Fig. 4: one shaded rectangle from the peak to the
    trough of each recession.

    Arguments
        fig   : the figure to shade
        start : a date; the recessions that end before it are left out
    Returns
        the same figure
    """
    # `zip(a, b)` hands over one pair of values at a time, here the peak and the
    # trough of each recession
    for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
        if trough >= pd.Timestamp(start):
            # `add_vrect` shades a vertical band from x0 to x1
            fig.add_vrect(
                x0=peak,
                x1=trough,
                fillcolor=BLUE,
                opacity=0.12,
                line_width=0,
            )
    return fig
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, components of private investment
def components_chart(frequency="annual"):
    """Investment and its components, percent of GDP, with recessions shaded.

    Draws Fig. 4 (inspired by Fig. 17.4 in Jones), from the annual or the quarterly
    long table.

    Arguments
        frequency : "annual" or "quarterly"
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the table and the title; the quarterly title reports the lowest quarter
    title = "Investment and its components: all of them fall in recessions"
    data = annual_long
    if frequency == "quarterly":
        title = (
            f"Quarterly data: total investment fell to {low.Total:.1f}% of GDP "
            f"in {low.date.year}Q{low.date.quarter}"
        )
        data = quarterly_long

    # Step 2: one line per component, in the colors of COLORS
    fig = px.line(
        data,
        x="date",
        y="share",
        color="component",
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        title=title,
        labels={"date": "Year", "share": "Percent of GDP", "component": "Component"},
    )
    # Step 3: the recession bands, and a black line at zero
    shade_recessions(fig, "1975-01-01")
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    # Step 4: fixed axes, and the legend inside the chart at the top left
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_range=["1975-01-01", "2026-12-31"],
        yaxis=dict(range=[-5, 25], tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25]),
        legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.01, y=0.99, title=None),
    )
    return fig

Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, NIPA Table 1.1.5, via FRED: gross private domestic investment (GPDIA), private nonresidential fixed investment (PNFIA), private residential fixed investment (PRFIA), change in private inventories (CBIA) and GDP (GDPA); quarterly shares of GDP from NIPA Table 1.1.10, via FRED (A006RE1Q156NBEA, A011RE1Q156NBEA); recessions: NBER business cycle dates, via FRED (USREC). Prepared files: data/ch17/fig17-4.csv, data/ch17/investment_quarterly.csv, data/ch17/recessions.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 17.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Total investment averaged 17.8 percent of GDP from 1975 to 2025, but it swings a lot: from 19.6 percent in 2006 to 13.3 percent in 2009, the lowest value in the figure.
  • Residential investment peaked at 6.6 percent of GDP in 2005 and fell to 2.4 percent in 2011, less than half: the housing bust of the Great Recession.
  • Inventory investment is small but procyclical: it was negative in the recession years 1975, 1980, 1982, 1991, 2001, 2008, 2009 and 2020, and in 1983, just after a recession. Firms run down their inventories when sales fall.
  • Click a name in the legend to hide or show that component. Click quarterly: the textbook’s “less than 13 percent of GDP in 2009” is a quarterly number; the annual value is 13.3.

Beyond the United States: investment in 35 countries

Do housing and inventories swing as much in other countries? The OECD’s national accounts let us build the same three parts for 35 countries, from 1970 or 1995 to the latest year:

  • private investment (total) is all fixed investment minus that of the government, plus inventory investment;
  • residential investment is the investment in dwellings (it also includes a little public housing);
  • nonresidential fixed investment is the rest of private fixed investment.

For the United States this gives the BEA’s numbers of fig17-4.csv within 0.4 points of GDP in every year.

# Load the OECD data: one row per country and year, with the three parts of investment
world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "investment_components.csv")
world.head(3)
iso3 country year total nonres_fixed residential inventories region

The chart function draws one country at a time, with the same names and colors as Fig. 4. The vertical axis keeps the textbook’s scale unless a country invests more than 25 percent of GDP; then it switches to a wider fixed scale.

First the numbers: country_components takes one country’s rows, makes the long table, and finds the years of the lowest and the highest private investment, which the title reports.

def country_components(country):
    """One country's investment and its parts, and its lowest and highest year.

    Private investment and its three parts, in percent of GDP, from the OECD's
    national accounts (the data of Fig. 4 for 35 countries).

    Arguments
        country : the country's name, as in `world`
    Returns
        long      : one row per year and component, in percent of GDP
        low, high : the rows of the years with the lowest and the highest total
    """
    # Step 1: the country's rows, with the names of Fig. 4
    rows = world[world.country == country].rename(columns=NAMES)
    # Step 2: the long table, one row per year and component
    long = rows.melt(
        id_vars=["iso3", "country", "year", "region"],
        var_name="component",
        value_name="share",
    )
    # Step 3: the years of the lowest and the highest total (`idxmin` and `idxmax`
    # give the row labels of the smallest and the largest value)
    low, high = rows.loc[rows.Total.idxmin()], rows.loc[rows.Total.idxmax()]
    return long, low, high
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, investment in one of 35 countries
def components_by_country(country="United States"):
    """Private investment and its parts in one country, percent of GDP (OECD, annual).

    Draws Fig. 4 for one country (inspired by Fig. 17.4 in Jones).

    Arguments
        country : the country's name, as in `world`
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (country_components)
    long, low, high = country_components(country)
    # Step 2: the textbook's scale, or a second, fixed scale for the
    # high-investment countries
    top = 25
    if high.Total > 25:
        top = 55

    # Step 3: one line per component, in the colors of Fig. 4
    fig = px.line(
        long,
        x="year",
        y="share",
        color="component",
        color_discrete_map=COLORS,
        hover_name="country",
        labels={"year": "Year", "share": "Percent of GDP", "component": "Component"},
        title=f"{country}: investment from {low.Total:.1f}% ({low.year}) to "
              f"{high.Total:.1f}% ({high.year}) of GDP",
    )
    # Step 4: a black line at zero, fixed axes, and the legend at the top left
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_range=[1969, 2026],
        yaxis=dict(range=[-5, top]),
        legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.01, y=0.99, title=None),
    )
    return fig

Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the website versions with a country menu (run it; no need to read)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, options, start):
    """Precompute make_figure(option) for every option and join them with a menu.

    The website cannot run Python, so a figure with a country menu (Fig. 4 for 35
    countries) gets this precomputed version: the traces of every option, and a
    dropdown menu that shows one option's traces at a time.

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure for one option
        options     : the options of the menu, e.g. the country names
        start       : the option shown first
    Returns
        a Plotly figure with a dropdown menu
    """
    # Step 1: one figure per option; the one shown first gives the layout
    figures = [make_figure(o) for o in options]
    first = options.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    # Step 2: all their traces in one figure; only those of `start` are visible
    owner = []                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one menu entry per option: it shows that option's traces, with its
    # title, axis range, annotations and shapes
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {
            "title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
            "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range,
            "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
            "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes],
        }
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(options[i]), method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    # Step 4: the menu above the chart, with room for it at the top
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", active=first, buttons=buttons, x=0, y=1.02,
                xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig

    sorted(world.country.unique()),
    start="United States",
)

What to notice.

  • Housing booms were not only American. Choose Ireland: its residential investment reached 13.5 percent of GDP in 2006, twice the U.S. peak, and fell to 2.0 percent in 2011. Greece’s reached 11.0 percent in 2007.
  • Germany had no housing boom in the 2000s. Its total still fell, to 15.1 percent of GDP in 2009, and inventories fell by 1.1 percent of GDP that year, as in Japan (−1.0). The recession of 2009 was worldwide.
  • Look at your data: Ireland’s investment jumps to 51.5 percent of GDP in 2019. Multinational firms moved their patents and other intellectual property to Ireland, which counts as investment there. It is accounting, not new factories.

Key numbers: which part of investment falls in a recession?

For four recessions we compute how much each part of investment changed, in percentage points of GDP, from the year before the recession to its worst year.

# The change of each part of investment, in points of GDP, in four recessions
# Step 1: one row per year; `.loc[year]` then picks the row of a year
table = invest.set_index("year")
# Step 2: for each episode, the change from the year before the recession to its
# worst year; `rows.append` adds it to the list
rows = []
for start, end in [(1979, 1982), (2000, 2002), (2006, 2009), (2019, 2020)]:
    change = table.loc[end] - table.loc[start]
    change["episode"] = f"{start} to {end}"
    rows.append(change)
# Step 3: the list of rows as one table, rounded to two decimals
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("episode").round(2)
Total Nonresidential fixed Residential Inventory
episode
1979 to 1982 -3.16 0.28 -2.31 -1.13
2000 to 2002 -2.22 -2.24 0.37 -0.35
2006 to 2009 -6.22 -1.31 -3.37 -1.54
2019 to 2020 -0.47 -0.46 0.47 -0.48

Every recession is different. Housing collapsed in the early 1980s, when interest rates were very high, and again in 2006–2009, when it explains more than half of the fall of 6.2 points. The dot-com bust of 2000–2002 hit business investment, while housing even grew. In 2020 the recession lasted only two months, so annual data hide most of it.

Key numbers: house prices and leverage

The arbitrage equation also prices a house. An investor can keep the down payment in the bank, or buy a condominium with a mortgage, rent it out for a year and sell it. Equating the two returns gives the house price of equation (13):

\[p^{\text{house}} = \frac{\text{rent}}{\tau\bar{x}R + (1-\tau)R + \bar{d} - \Delta p^{\text{house}}/p^{\text{house}}}\]

where \(\bar{x}\) is the down payment as a share of the price and \(\tau\) the tax rate at which mortgage interest can be deducted. We use illustrative numbers: a rent of 6,000 dollars a year, \(R = 4\) percent, \(\bar{d} = 2\) percent, \(\tau = 0.3\) and expected price growth of 2 percent.

def house_price(rent, R, d, gp, tau, x):
    """The price of a house, from the arbitrage equation.

    Equation (13):  price = rent / (tau x R + (1 - tau) R + d - gp)

    Arguments
        rent : the rent, dollars a year
        R    : real interest rate, R
        d    : depreciation rate, d-bar
        gp   : the expected growth of the house price
        tau  : the tax rate at which mortgage interest can be deducted
        x    : the down payment as a share of the price, x-bar
    Returns
        the price of the house, in dollars
    """
    # the rent divided by the user cost of the house
    return rent / (tau * x * R + (1 - tau) * R + d - gp)


# Step 1: the baseline price (":,.0f" writes the thousands with commas)
base = house_price(6000, 0.04, 0.02, 0.02, 0.3, 0.2)
print(f"Baseline price (20% down payment, 2% price growth): {base:,.0f} dollars")
# Step 2: the change in the price when the down payment falls to 10 percent, and
# when expected price growth rises to 3 percent
print(
    "Down payment falls to 10%:          "
    f"{house_price(6000, 0.04, 0.02, 0.02, 0.3, 0.1) / base - 1:+.1%}"
)
print(
    "Expected price growth rises to 3%:  "
    f"{house_price(6000, 0.04, 0.02, 0.03, 0.3, 0.2) / base - 1:+.1%}"
)
Baseline price (20% down payment, 2% price growth): 197,368 dollars
Down payment falls to 10%:          +4.1%
Expected price growth rises to 3%:  +49.0%

With these numbers, cheaper credit (a smaller down payment) raises the price by about 4 percent, but a belief that prices will grow 1 point faster raises it by about half. Expected capital gains can feed on themselves, which is how a housing bubble grows.

17.6 Concluding remarks

  • The arbitrage equation, equation (1), says that two equally safe investments must earn the same return. Applied to physical capital, it says that a firm keeps adding capital as long as its marginal product is above the user cost of capital, \(R + \bar{d} - \Delta p_k/p_k\) (equation 2), and stops where the two are equal.
  • A corporate income tax divides the user cost by \(1-\tau\) (equation 3).
  • With diminishing returns, equations (4) and (5) turn the user cost into a desired capital stock proportional to \(uc^{-3/2}\), and equations (6) and (7) into a capital-output ratio \(Y/K = 3\cdot uc\) and an investment rate \((g_K + \bar{d})/(3\cdot uc)\). A 35 percent tax cuts desired capital by about half and the investment rate by 35 percent.
  • Applied to stocks, the same equation, (8), gives \(p_s = \text{dividend}/(R-g)\) (equation 9): a stock is worth the present value of its dividends. The P/E ratio of equation (10) then depends on \(R-g\), which makes it very sensitive to expected growth and hard to use for spotting bubbles.
  • Tobin’s \(q\), equations (11) and (12), links the stock market to investment: \(q > 1\) exactly when the marginal product of capital is above the user cost. The house price of equation (13) shows how leverage, the mortgage tax deduction and, above all, expected price gains move house prices.
  • In the data, total investment and especially housing and inventories fall sharply in recessions.
  • The next chapter turns to the government and the macroeconomy: how governments spend, tax and borrow, and what their budget constraint implies for debt and deficits.

Practice problems

These problems put the chapter to work in three ways: conceptual problems apply the arbitrage equation to real cases, data-based problems send you back to the chapter’s data, and modeling problems use the interactive models to answer policy questions. Each problem is marked Basic, Intermediate or Challenge: try it on your own first, then open the Hint, and only then the Solution. The sliders of the modeling problems run in Colab (open the notebook with the badge at the top); on the website, use the website version of each figure above.

Conceptual problems

Problem 1 (Basic): A minimum tax for Ireland’s multinationals. Ireland taxes company profits at 12.5 percent, one of the lowest rates in the tax table after Fig. 2. In October 2021 most members of the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework agreed that multinational groups with a revenue of at least 750 million euros should pay a tax rate of at least 15 percent (OECD statement), and Ireland now charges such groups a top-up tax that brings them to that rate (Revenue, the Irish tax agency). Keep the user cost before taxes of 7.9 percent that the tax table uses.

  1. Use equation (3) to compute the user cost of capital of a large multinational in Ireland, first with a tax rate of 12.5 percent and then with 15 percent.

  2. By what percentage does its desired capital stock change? Use equation (5).

  3. By what percentage does its investment rate, equation (7), change? Is the minimum tax a big deal for the machines and buildings that multinationals own in Ireland?

Hint

The user cost is \(0.079/(1-\tau)\). Desired capital is proportional to \(uc^{-3/2}\) and the investment rate to \(1/uc\), so for (b) and (c) you only need the ratio of the two user costs, \((1-0.125)/(1-0.15)\).

Your answer:

Solution

(a) Equation (3) divides the user cost before taxes by the share of income the firm keeps, \(1-\tau\):

\[uc_{12.5} = \frac{0.079}{1-0.125} = \frac{0.079}{0.875} \approx 0.0903, \qquad uc_{15} = \frac{0.079}{1-0.15} = \frac{0.079}{0.85} \approx 0.0929.\]

The user cost rises from 9.03 to 9.29 percent, by the factor \(0.875/0.85 \approx 1.029\), that is by 2.9 percent.

(b) Equation (5) makes desired capital proportional to \(uc^{-3/2}\), and nothing else in it changes:

\[\frac{K_{15}}{K_{12.5}} = \left(\frac{uc_{12.5}}{uc_{15}}\right)^{3/2} = \left(\frac{0.85}{0.875}\right)^{3/2} \approx 0.957.\]

Desired capital falls by about 4.3 percent. The elasticity of \(-1.5\) gives almost the same answer: \(-1.5 \times 2.9 \approx -4.4\) percent.

(c) Equation (7) makes the investment rate proportional to \(1/uc\), so it falls by the factor \(0.85/0.875 \approx 0.971\), or by 2.9 percent: an investment rate of 20 percent of output would become about 19.4 percent.

These are small effects. A rise of 2.5 points in the tax rate changes the share the firm keeps only from 0.875 to 0.85. The minimum tax matters much more for where multinationals report their profits than for where they build factories: recall from Fig. 4 that Ireland’s measured investment jumped in 2019 when firms moved their intellectual property there, an accounting move rather than new machines.

Problem 2 (Intermediate): Why did U.S. house prices hold up in 2022–23? Real interest rates in the United States rose fast after 2021. The yield on 10-year inflation-indexed Treasury bonds, a measure of the real interest rate, averaged −0.91 percent in 2021 and 1.68 percent in 2023 (FRED, DFII10), a rise of about 2.6 points. Yet real house prices did not fall: the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index (FRED, CSUSHPISA), divided by the consumer price index (FRED, CPIAUCSL), was 4.6 percent higher in 2023 than in 2021 (our calculation from the annual averages).

  1. Start from the house of the Key numbers after Fig. 4: a rent of 6,000 dollars a year, \(R = 0.04\), \(\bar{d} = 0.02\), \(\tau = 0.3\), \(\bar{x} = 0.2\) and expected price growth of 2 percent. Raise \(R\) by 2.6 points. What price does equation (13) predict, and how large is the fall?

  2. By how many points would expected price growth, \(\Delta P^{\text{house}}/P^{\text{house}}\), have had to rise to keep the price unchanged?

  3. In the model, every buyer borrows at today’s rate \(R\). In practice, many U.S. owners hold 30-year fixed-rate mortgages taken out when rates were low: the average 30-year fixed rate was 2.96 percent in 2021 and 6.81 percent in 2023 (Freddie Mac, via FRED, MORTGAGE30US). Why might this keep house prices up when rates rise?

Hint
  1. Only the interest terms of the denominator change, by \((\tau\bar{x} + 1 - \tau)\,\Delta R\) (see the table after equation (13)). (b) Expected price growth enters the denominator with a minus sign and a coefficient of one. (c) Would you sell your house if moving meant swapping a 3 percent loan for a 7 percent one?

Your answer:

Solution

(a) At the start, the denominator of equation (13) is

\[\tau\bar{x}R + (1-\tau)R + \bar{d} - \frac{\Delta P^{\text{house}}}{P^{\text{house}}} = 0.3\times0.2\times0.04 + 0.7\times0.04 + 0.02 - 0.02 = 0.0024 + 0.028 = 0.0304,\]

so the price is \(6{,}000/0.0304 \approx 197{,}368\) dollars. With \(R = 0.066\) the denominator becomes

\[0.3\times0.2\times0.066 + 0.7\times0.066 + 0.02 - 0.02 = 0.00396 + 0.0462 = 0.05016,\]

and the price \(6{,}000/0.05016 \approx 119{,}617\) dollars, a fall of 39.4 percent. A shortcut: the interest terms add up to \((\tau\bar{x} + 1 - \tau)R = 0.76\,R\), so the denominator rises by \(0.76 \times 0.026 = 0.01976\). Because the denominator is a small number, this adds 65 percent to it. The model predicts a housing crash.

(b) To keep the price, the denominator must stay at 0.0304. Expected price growth enters it with a coefficient of \(-1\), so it must rise by as much as the interest terms did: \(0.76 \times 0.026 \approx 0.020\), about 2 points, from 2 to 4 percent a year after inflation. To match the 4.6 percent rise in real prices, the denominator must fall to \(0.0304/1.046 \approx 0.0291\), which needs expected growth of 4.1 percent, 2.1 points more than before. So the model fits the facts only if buyers became much more optimistic about house prices at the very moment interest rates jumped. That is possible, but it is a strong assumption.

(c) An owner with a 3 percent loan who sells her house must repay that loan, and pay about 7 percent on the loan for her next home. Many owners therefore stayed where they were, and few houses came on the market. Fewer sellers support the price, which the model leaves out, because it assumes that anyone can buy or sell at no cost. Batzer, Coste, Doerner and Seiler (2024), economists at the Federal Housing Finance Agency, estimate that this “lock-in” prevented about 1.33 million home sales between the second quarter of 2022 and the end of 2023, and that the smaller supply raised prices by 5.7 percent, more than the 3.3 percent by which the higher rates lowered them directly. The arbitrage equation still pulls prices toward equation (13), but when buying and selling are costly, it can take years.

Data-based problems

Problem 3 (Intermediate): The race to the bottom in corporate taxes. Many governments cut their corporate tax rates after 2000. Check this with corporate_tax.csv, which holds the statutory tax rates of the central government from the OECD’s Corporate Tax Statistics (OECD Data Explorer), for the 33 jurisdictions of the tax table after Fig. 2. Use 2025 as the last year, because one jurisdiction has no rate for 2026 yet.

  1. What was the average rate of the 33 jurisdictions in 2000, and in 2025? How many of them cut their rate, kept it, or raised it?

  2. Which three jurisdictions made the biggest cuts?

  3. Keep the user cost before taxes fixed. Equations (3) and (5) then say that desired capital is proportional to \((1-\tau)^{3/2}\). By what factor did the change in its tax rate raise each jurisdiction’s desired capital stock between 2000 and 2025? Report the median factor and the three largest ones.

Hint

rates.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="cit_rate") turns the long table into a wide one, with one row per country and one column per year. Then rate_change = wide[2025] - wide[2000] is a column of changes, and (rate_change < 0).sum() counts the cuts, because Python counts each True as 1. The rates are in percent: divide them by 100 before you use them in \((1-\tau)^{3/2}\).

# Your answer here
Solution

We read the file, give each year its own column with pivot, and compare the columns for 2000 and 2025.

rates = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "corporate_tax.csv")
wide = rates.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="cit_rate")    # one row per country
rate_change = wide[2025] - wide[2000]
print(f"Average rate: {wide[2000].mean():.1f}% in 2000, {wide[2025].mean():.1f}% in 2025")
print(f"Cut: {(rate_change < 0).sum()}, unchanged: {(rate_change == 0).sum()}, raised: {(rate_change > 0).sum()}")
print("Raised:", list(rate_change[rate_change > 0].index))
print(f"Standard deviation: {wide[2000].std():.1f} points in 2000, {wide[2025].std():.1f} in 2025")
print(rate_change.sort_values().head(3).round(1))

The average rate fell from 30.7 percent in 2000 to 23.8 percent in 2025. Twenty-five jurisdictions cut their rate, six kept it and only two raised it, Chile and Hong Kong. The biggest cuts were made by India (27.2 points), Germany (26.4) and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (20.0).

For (c), desired capital is proportional to \((1-\tau)^{3/2}\), so the factor is \(\left((1-\tau_{2025})/(1-\tau_{2000})\right)^{3/2}\):

factor = ((1 - wide[2025] / 100) / (1 - wide[2000] / 100)) ** 1.5      # equations (3) and (5)
print(f"Median factor: {factor.median():.2f}")
print(factor.sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).round(2))

The median factor is 1.12: for the typical jurisdiction, the tax cuts alone raised desired capital by about 12 percent. India’s factor is 1.97, Germany’s 1.76 and Congo’s 1.66, so in the model their tax cuts almost doubled the capital stock that firms want. Chile, with a factor of 0.80, went the other way.

Two cautions. First, the file holds the central government’s rate only, so taxes that regions or cities charge on profits are left out (see the data notes). Second, the factors assume that nothing else in the tax code changed, such as the deductions that firms may claim. Still, the pattern is clear: rates fell almost everywhere, and the spread between them narrowed (the standard deviation fell from 10.1 to 7.5 points), which is what you would expect if countries compete for capital.

Problem 4 (Challenge): Does housing warn of recessions? Edward Leamer argued that, of all the parts of GDP, residential investment gives the best early warning of a U.S. recession (Leamer 2007, NBER Working Paper 13428). Test his claim with the quarterly shares of GDP in investment_quarterly.csv (BEA, NIPA Table 1.1.10, via FRED: residential A011RE1Q156NBEA and total A006RE1Q156NBEA) and the recession dates in recessions.csv (NBER business cycle dates).

  1. For each of the 12 recessions since 1948, compute the change in the residential share of GDP over the year before the recession, from four quarters before the peak to the quarter that contains the peak. Do the same for the share of total investment. Before how many recessions did each share fall?

  2. Leamer noted that housing gave no warning of the recessions that began in 1953 and 2001. Do our numbers agree?

  3. Compute the same four-quarter change for the first quarter of 2023. The NBER list has no recession after 2020. Was this a false alarm? Use equation (13) and Problem 2 to explain why housing fell first, and what else would be needed for a recession.

Hint

Loop over dates.peak. For each peak, housing[housing.date <= peak] keeps the quarters up to the one that contains the peak; .iloc[-1] is that last quarter and .iloc[-5] the quarter one year earlier. Round each change to one decimal before you test whether it is below zero.

# Your answer here
Solution

For each peak we take the last quarter that starts on or before the peak month, and the quarter four rows earlier, and subtract their shares.

housing = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "investment_quarterly.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
dates = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])
housing_falls, total_falls = 0, 0
for peak in dates.peak:
    before = housing[housing.date <= peak]         # every quarter up to the one with the peak
    now, year_ago = before.iloc[-1], before.iloc[-5]
    res = round(now.residential - year_ago.residential, 1) + 0.0
    tot = round(now.total - year_ago.total, 1) + 0.0
    if res < 0:
        housing_falls += 1
    if tot < 0:
        total_falls += 1
    print(f"Peak {peak:%b %Y}: residential {res:+.1f}, total {tot:+.1f} points of GDP")
print(f"Falls in the year before a peak: residential {housing_falls} of 12, total {total_falls} of 12")

The residential share fell in the year before 11 of the 12 recessions; the exception is 2020, when the recession came with the COVID-19 pandemic (NBER announcement). The share of total investment fell before only 8 of them, and it even rose before the recessions of 1948, 1953, 1973 and 1981. Housing is the better warning, as Leamer said. The falls are often half a point or more: 0.6 before 1957, 0.7 before 1960, 1973 and 1980, and 1.4 before December 2007, at the start of the Great Recession.

(b) Yes. Before July 1953 and March 2001 the residential share fell by only 0.1 point, too little to count as a warning. Leamer traces those two recessions to other causes, the cut in defense spending after the Korean armistice and the end of the internet boom; in 2000–2002 it was business investment that collapsed (see the Key numbers after Fig. 4).

(c)

q2022 = housing[housing.date == "2022-01-01"].residential.iloc[0]
q2023 = housing[housing.date == "2023-01-01"].residential.iloc[0]
print(f"Residential share: {q2022:.1f}% in 2022Q1, {q2023:.1f}% in 2023Q1, change {q2023 - q2022:+.1f} points")
rest_2022 = housing[housing.date == "2022-01-01"].total.iloc[0] - q2022
rest_2023 = housing[housing.date == "2023-01-01"].total.iloc[0] - q2023
print(f"Rest of private investment: {rest_2022:.1f}% -> {rest_2023:.1f}% of GDP")

The residential share fell from 4.8 to 4.0 percent of GDP, a drop of 0.8 points, as large as before most recessions, and no recession followed in our data. It was a false alarm. Housing fell first because its user cost, the denominator of equation (13), reacts most to the interest rate: Problem 2 showed that 2.6 more points of real interest rate raise it by 65 percent. In Leamer’s account, a recession follows when the slump in housing spreads to the rest of the economy, starting with spending on consumer durables. In 2022–23 the rest of private investment (total minus residential) fell only from 14.2 to 13.9 percent of GDP. A single indicator can warn, but it cannot prove that a recession is coming.

Modeling problems

Problem 5 (Basic): Buy machines before the tariff? Firms often rush to buy before a price rise. In early 2025 the staff of the Federal Reserve linked a surge in U.S. imports to purchases made ahead of expected tariff increases (FOMC minutes, May 2025), and U.S. equipment investment grew at an annual rate of 22.5 percent in the first quarter, in the BEA’s first estimate (BEA, Survey of Current Business, May 2025). Take a hypothetical firm in Fig. 1’s model, with \(R = 0.02\), \(\bar{d} = 0.08\) and \(\bar{A} = 0.3\), which holds its desired capital stock, \(K_0 = 1\). A tariff announced for next year makes the firm expect the price of its machines to rise by 3 percent during this year.

  1. Move the slider for the expected price rise from 0 to 0.03. What happens to the user cost, the desired capital stock and this year’s investment?

  2. Once the tariff is in place, machine prices stop rising. Set the price rise back to 0, and the starting capital to the capital the firm owns after (a). What does the firm invest in the following year?

Hint

All three numbers are in the title of the chart. An expected rise in the price of a machine is a capital gain, so it enters the user cost of equation (2) with a minus sign. In (b), the firm’s capital is the desired capital you read in (a), rounded to the slider’s step of 0.1.

interact(desired_capital_diagram,
         R=fixed(0.02), d=fixed(0.08), A=fixed(A_BAR),
         gpk=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=0.0, max=0.04, step=0.01, description="expected price rise Δp/p", style=WIDE),
         K0=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.1, description="starting capital K0", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 1 above, adapted from Fig. 17.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here
Solution

(a) The title changes from “User cost 10.0% | desired capital 1.00 | investment from K0 = 1.0: +0.08” to “User cost 7.0% | desired capital 1.71 | investment from K0 = 1.0: +0.79”. A machine bought today can be sold dearer at the end of the year, so owning it costs 3 points less, and the user cost falls from \(0.02 + 0.08 = 0.10\) to \(0.02 + 0.08 - 0.03 = 0.07\). Equation (5) turns this 30 percent cut in the user cost into a 71 percent rise in desired capital, \((0.10/0.07)^{3/2} \approx 1.71\). Investment, which normally only replaces the 8 percent of capital that wears out each year, becomes almost ten times larger: \(1.71 - 0.92 \times 1 \approx 0.79\).

(b) With \(\Delta p/p = 0\) and \(K_0 = 1.7\) the title shows investment of \(-0.56\) (with the exact 1.71, \(1 - 0.92 \times 1.71 \approx -0.57\)). The firm now owns more capital than it wants, so it buys no machines at all and lets depreciation shrink its capital. You can check the numbers in the answer cell:

uc_gain = user_cost(0.02, 0.08, gpk=0.03)
K_boom = desired_capital(uc_gain)
print(f"This year: user cost {uc_gain:.2f}, desired capital {K_boom:.3f}, investment {K_boom - 0.92 * 1.0:.3f}")
print(f"Next year: investment {desired_capital(user_cost(0.02, 0.08)) - 0.92 * K_boom:.3f}")

It prints a user cost of 0.07, desired capital of 1.707 and investment of 0.787 this year, and \(-0.571\) the year after. With no new machines, capital shrinks by 8 percent a year, so it takes 7 years to fall back from 1.71 to 1. (Strictly, the machines also stay 3 percent dearer after the tariff, which raises the user cost to 0.103 and lowers desired capital a little further, to about 0.96.)

The policy lesson. An announced price rise does not create investment out of nothing: it moves investment forward in time, a boom this year and a bust after it. Real firms face costs of installing machines quickly, so the boom is spread out and smaller than in our model, but its direction is the same. The same logic applies to a temporary investment subsidy: when firms know that it ends next year, they bring their purchases forward.

Problem 6 (Intermediate): Can the central bank cool the stock market? In our data, which end in October 2026, Shiller’s P/E ratio is 40.7, more than twice its long-run average of 17.8 (see the title of Fig. 3). Could higher interest rates bring stock prices back down? Use the sliders below, with the payout ratio fixed at one half.

  1. Set \(R = 4\) percent. Which dividend growth rate \(g\) on the slider brings the model’s P/E ratio closest to the ratio of October 2026?

  2. The central bank now raises the real interest rate by one point, to \(R = 5\) percent, and expected growth does not change. What P/E ratio does the model predict, and by what percentage would stock prices fall?

  3. Repeat (b) for a market at its long-run average: with a payout ratio of one half, a P/E ratio of 17.8 implies \(R - g = 0.5/17.8\). By what percentage would prices fall after the same one-point rise? Why is the answer so different?

  4. Higher interest rates also reach investment. Take the firm of Fig. 1, with \(R = 2\) percent, which holds its desired capital \(K = 1\). Use tobin_q to compute its \(q\) after a rise of the interest rate to 3 percent, and desired_capital with user_cost to find its new desired capital. What will the firm do?

Hint

By equation (10), the P/E ratio is \(0.5/(R-g)\), so a P/E ratio of 40.7 needs \(R - g = 0.5/40.7\). In (b) and (c), prices fall by the factor \((R-g)_{\text{before}}/(R-g)_{\text{after}}\). In (d), use tobin_q(1.0, R=0.03) and desired_capital(user_cost(0.03, 0.08)).

interact(pe_chart,
         R=FloatSlider(value=0.04, min=0.03, max=0.06, step=0.005, description="interest rate R", style=WIDE, readout_format=".3f"),
         g=FloatSlider(value=0.02, min=0.0, max=0.035, step=0.0025, description="dividend growth g", style=WIDE, readout_format=".4f"),
         payout=fixed(0.5));

Source. The chart of Fig. 3 above: data from Robert J. Shiller, Online Data; the model line of equation (10) is adapted from the discussion of Fig. 17.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here
Solution

(a) The P/E ratio of 40.7 needs \(R - g = 0.5/40.7 \approx 1.23\) percent, so \(g \approx 2.77\) percent. On the slider, \(g = 0.0275\) is closest: the title shows a model ratio of \(0.5/(0.04 - 0.0275) = 0.5/0.0125 = 40.0\).

(b) With \(R = 0.05\) the gap widens to \(R - g = 0.05 - 0.0275 = 0.0225\), and the model ratio falls to \(0.5/0.0225 \approx 22.2\). Since the price is proportional to \(1/(R-g)\), it falls by the factor \(0.0125/0.0225 \approx 0.556\): stock prices would fall by 44.4 percent.

(c) At the long-run average, \(R - g = 0.5/17.8 \approx 2.81\) percent. One more point gives 3.81 percent and a P/E ratio of \(0.5/0.0381 \approx 13.1\), so prices fall by the factor \(0.0281/0.0381\), that is by 26.3 percent. The same one-point rise does much less harm, because the price has an elasticity of \(-1\) with respect to the gap \(R-g\): one point is 80 percent of a gap of 1.25 points, but only 36 percent of a gap of 2.81 points. A market priced on a thin gap between interest rates and expected growth is very sensitive to interest rates.

(d)

print(f"P/E ratio: {pe_ratio(0.5, 0.04, 0.0275):.1f} -> {pe_ratio(0.5, 0.05, 0.0275):.1f}")
print(f"Tobin's q at R = 3%: {tobin_q(1.0, R=0.03):.3f}")
print(f"New desired capital: {desired_capital(user_cost(0.03, 0.08)):.3f}")

It prints 40.0 → 22.2, a \(q\) of 0.667 and a new desired capital stock of 0.867. With \(q\) below 1 the firm is worth less than its machines: it stops investing until depreciation has brought its capital down by about 13 percent, which takes two years at 8 percent a year. (Parts (a)–(c) use the stock example of the Model overview, with \(R\) around 4 to 5 percent; part (d) uses the machine baseline of Fig. 1, with \(R = 2\) percent.)

The policy answer. In the model, a central bank that raises real interest rates can bring stock prices down a lot, and through \(q\) it also lowers investment, which is one way monetary policy cools the economy. But the size of the fall depends on how thin the gap \(R - g\) is, which nobody observes directly. A central bank that tries to target stock prices could easily do far more, or far less, than it intends.

Problem 7 (Challenge): A Laffer curve for the corporate tax? Does a higher corporate tax always raise more revenue? Take Fig. 2’s economy: firms hold their desired capital stock, and the interest rate \(R = 0.02\) is set outside the country, for example on world capital markets. The government collects \(\tau\cdot MPK\cdot K\), and the title of the chart below adds output and this tax revenue.

  1. Move the slider from 5 to 70 percent. At which tax rate on the slider is the revenue highest?

  2. Show that revenue is \(T = \frac{\tau}{3}\,Y\) and that output at the desired capital stock is \(Y = \bar{A}L\left(\frac{\bar{A}(1-\tau)}{3\,uc_0}\right)^{1/2}\), where \(uc_0 = R + \bar{d}\) is the user cost without the tax. Then derive the tax rate that maximizes revenue.

  3. Workers earn the other two thirds of output. At \(\tau = 0.35\), compare the tax revenue with the fall in wages, relative to an economy with no corporate tax. Who pays the corporate tax in this model?

  4. The rates of our tax table run from 0 to about 36 percent in 2025, far below your answer to (b). Give two reasons why.

Hint
  1. Equation (4) says \(MPK\cdot K = \frac{1}{3}Y\). Put \(K^{\text{desired}}\) from equation (5), with \(uc = uc_0/(1-\tau)\), into \(Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}\). With the baseline, \(\bar{A}/(3\,uc_0) = 1\), so revenue is proportional to \(\tau(1-\tau)^{1/2}\): set its derivative to zero. (c) Wages are \(\frac{2}{3}Y\); compare them with and without the tax.
def tax_revenue_diagram(tau=0.35):
    """Fig. 2 with output and the tax revenue tau x MPK x K at the desired capital stock in the title."""
    fig = corporate_tax_diagram(tau, R=0.02, d=0.08)
    K1 = desired_capital(user_cost(0.02, 0.08, tau=tau))
    Y1 = A_BAR * K1 ** (1 / 3) * L_BAR ** (2 / 3)
    revenue = tau * mpk(K1) * K1
    fig.update_layout(title=f"τ = {tau:.0%}  |  desired capital {K1:.2f}  |  output {Y1:.3f}  |  tax revenue {revenue:.4f}")
    return fig


interact(tax_revenue_diagram,
         tau=FloatSlider(value=0.35, min=0.05, max=0.7, step=0.05, description="corporate tax rate τ", style=WIDE));

Source. The model of Fig. 2 above, with a tax-revenue readout of our own, adapted from Fig. 17.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

# Your answer here
Solution

(a) Revenue rises from 0.0049 at 5 percent to 0.0282 at 35 percent and 0.0385 at 65 percent, then falls to 0.0383 at 70 percent. On the slider, 65 percent raises the most.

(b) At the desired capital stock, equation (4) gives \(MPK = \frac{1}{3}Y/K\), so revenue is

\[T = \tau\cdot MPK\cdot K = \frac{\tau}{3}\,Y.\]

From equation (5), \(K = L\left(\bar{A}/(3\,uc)\right)^{3/2}\), so \(K^{1/3} = L^{1/3}\left(\bar{A}/(3\,uc)\right)^{1/2}\) and

\[Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3} = \bar{A}L\left(\frac{\bar{A}}{3\,uc}\right)^{1/2} = \bar{A}L\left(\frac{\bar{A}(1-\tau)}{3\,uc_0}\right)^{1/2},\]

using \(uc = uc_0/(1-\tau)\) from equation (3). With the baseline, \(\bar{A} = 0.3\), \(L = 1\) and \(uc_0 = 0.10\), the ratio \(\bar{A}/(3\,uc_0)\) is 1, so \(Y = 0.3\,(1-\tau)^{1/2}\) and \(T = 0.1\,\tau(1-\tau)^{1/2}\). The tax raises revenue on each unit of output but shrinks output. Setting the derivative to zero,

\[\frac{dT}{d\tau} = 0.1\left[(1-\tau)^{1/2} - \frac{\tau}{2}(1-\tau)^{-1/2}\right] = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2(1-\tau) = \tau \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tau^* = \frac{2}{3},\]

after multiplying the bracket by \(2(1-\tau)^{1/2}\). At \(\tau^* = 2/3\), revenue is \(0.1\times\frac{2}{3}\times(1/3)^{1/2} \approx 0.0385\), and output is \(0.3\times(1/3)^{1/2} \approx 0.173\), 42 percent below its level with no tax. Below 2/3, where every rate of our tax table lies, a tax cut loses revenue: it does not pay for itself. Only above 2/3 would a cut raise revenue.

(c) With no tax, output is 0.3 and wages are \(\frac{2}{3}\times0.3 = 0.2\). At \(\tau = 0.35\), output is \(0.3\times0.65^{1/2} \approx 0.2419\), so wages fall to about 0.1612, a loss of 0.0388, while the government collects only 0.0282. Workers lose 1.37 dollars of wages for each dollar of revenue.

Y_no_tax = A_BAR * desired_capital(user_cost(0.02, 0.08)) ** (1 / 3)
K35 = desired_capital(user_cost(0.02, 0.08, tau=0.35))
Y35 = A_BAR * K35 ** (1 / 3)
wage_loss = 2 / 3 * (Y_no_tax - Y35)
revenue_35 = 0.35 * mpk(K35) * K35
print(f"Output {Y_no_tax:.4f} -> {Y35:.4f}, wages fall by {wage_loss:.4f}, revenue {revenue_35:.4f}")
print(f"Wages lost per dollar of revenue: {wage_loss / revenue_35:.2f}")

In this model, the workers pay the corporate tax, and more than all of it. Because \(R\) is fixed, the owners of capital still earn \(R\) after tax: they simply invest less. With less capital per worker, the marginal product of labor and the wage fall.

(d) First, the revenue-maximizing rate is not the best rate: at 2/3, output would be 42 percent lower, and (c) shows that workers lose more in wages than the government collects (in this model, that is true at every positive rate). Second, capital and profits move between countries. Problem 3 showed that most countries cut their rates after 2000, and Problem 1 that firms can report their profits where taxes are low; a country with a rate far above its neighbors would lose part of its tax base.
